items.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006
items.q: With the Improvisational Arts Quintet, that’s the group I play with Kidd and Alvin Fielder

ctx.x: You know I think the average person when they think of New Orleans music they probably typecast it into well yes, I know Dixieland jazz came from there and maybe a little of the Neville Brothers. I don’t know, I count myself in this category, that I didn’t realize how much — different kinds of things were actually coming out of New Orleans.

Right. And even now as we try to rebuild and regroup, there’s been a part of New Orleans music and New Orleans culture for instance that has not been embraced and mainly it’s the really avante garde sorry to say. I don’t like the word but that’s the type of musician Kidd Jordan is. The kind of musician I am too because I can do that as well as play, because it’s all the same thing. But unless you sound something like Louis Armstrong or whatever like that man, it’s like it doesn’t matter. Whatever you do it…

and react among ourselves. And to me that’s the whole essence of improvisation. There’s no chords, no particular form, you just make it up as you go. And when you can come together and have those moments like that more, you can’t beat that you know. But New Orleans hasn’t embraced that. To me I think New Orleans is confused or they can’t look at the real thing about playing traditional music, creating music or creating music and the tradition that it was created. What I mean by that, if Louis Armstrong wouldn’t…
